title: The scratch in the gym
hookLine: someone scratches you in training; you don't suspect him forever (Meditations 6.20)

cards: Pickup basketball, Saturday morning. Going for a rebound, a guy catches you with an elbow, right in the ribs. It hurts.
He says, sorry, man. And here's the strange thing: you don't go home and lie awake wondering what he really meant, or tell your friends he's out to get you. It's the game.
Bodies collide. Now move that same elbow into an office, a family, a group chat, and suddenly it's a plot. Marcus Aurelius noticed the difference on the training ground.

teach.b: In Meditations six, twenty, Marcus describes training in the gymnasium. Someone scratches you with his nails, or butts you with his head. You don't make a show of anger.
You aren't offended. And you don't suspect him afterward of plotting against you. Marcus is not naive.
You do keep an eye on him next time, he says, but not as an enemy, and not with suspicion: with good-natured care, the way you'd step around a puppy that jumps. Watchful, not hostile.
Then the move: let it be like this in the rest of life too.
Overlook a lot in the people who are, so to speak, training alongside you. It's possible, he says, to step out of the way without suspecting or hating anyone.
In training, everyone knows bumps come with the sport; nobody expected a world without contact.
Life with other people is a contact sport too. A coworker forgets to cc you. A friend cancels.
Your sister says the thing in the wrong tone. Plenty of these are elbows under a rebound, not schemes. Marcus isn't saying nobody ever means harm.
He's saying the scratch shouldn't grow into a story. Treat it as what it probably was, and keep playing.

how: Readers of Marcus often use the gym image to keep small slights at their actual size: they stay alert to a pattern without assuming hostile intent from a single bump.

o: a training ground where bumps aren't taken as plots
an arena where gladiators fought before crowds
a bathhouse where Romans went to rest and talk

games.q: the scratch in the gym — tap the pairs.
p: watch him, not as an enemy
what the scratch shouldn't grow into

s: Marcus says never be careful around someone who hurt you
he says keep an eye on him, but without suspicion or hatred.
the passage describes being scratched or butted while training in the gymnasium
and not suspecting the other person of plotting afterward.
Marcus says nobody ever means harm
he says most bumps can be stepped around without suspicion; he doesn't deny that harm exists.

games.q: your training partner catches you with an elbow. it hurts. what do you do next session?
o: keep an eye out, but treat him as a friend, not an enemy.
tell everyone he did it on purpose.
games.why: Meditations 6.20: we watch out for him, but not as an enemy and without suspicion, and we can do the same in life.

practice: Think of a small hurt from the past week, a careless word, a missed reply, a bump in a crowded doorway, and notice whether you've built a story around it.
Picture it as an elbow in a pickup game, clumsy and part of being near people, and let the story shrink back to the size of the scratch.

wordCard.voice: Gymnasium. Marcus's training ground, where a scratch or a bump isn't a plot, and most of life's bumps aren't either. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a training ground, where athletes exercised; the setting Marcus pictures in 6.20.

carryVoice: Your line: just a scratch. Watchful, not hostile. See you on the court tomorrow.
